gap: No result ChatGPT got sets TechGearLab's figures beside the makers' specs. Read that way, ChatGPT's 'best budget' pick, the SIRUI Traveler 5C, got the lowest stability sub-score of the three tested candidates (5.0, against 7.4 for the Manfrotto Befree Advanced and 7.0 for the Peak Design Travel Tripod), with a tester reporting centre-column flex for long exposures. Also, the Peak Design (aluminum) weighed 3.68 lb in TechGearLab's table against Peak Design's stated 3.44 lb.
standout_why: I compared against the cited Amateur Photographer page (it returned HTTP 403 and could not be read), the cited digitalnomads.world page and the cited findingtheuniverse.com page, plus Pack Hacker and TechGearLab from the results. digitalnomads.world says outright it ran no wind, vibration or overload tests and uses only maker specs. findingtheuniverse.com says its table is all maker specs and gives no measured figures. Pack Hacker gives spec-sheet weights and mislabels its Peak Design figure: 3.432 lb is the aluminum spec, but it calls it carbon. TechGearLab ranked 11th in ChatGPT's first chat but was not cited, and it does hold the stability sub-scores, setup times and a 'Measured Weight' column. So the raw numbers are in one result ChatGPT got. No result lines them up against the maker specs or ties them to ChatGPT's four picks. No named reviewer published a measured settle time, vibration figure or scale weight for any of the four candidates, and nobody measured the Ulanzi Zero Y.
decides: This confirms the Manfrotto Befree Advanced over the SIRUI Traveler 5C for anyone shooting long exposures or using heavier lenses. TechGearLab scored the Befree highest overall (80) and highest on stability (7.4). The 5C scored 74 overall and 5.0 on stability, with a tester noting centre-column flex. The 5C remains the light, cheap pick: 1.9 lb in TechGearLab's table and 13 in folded. The Peak Design (aluminum) scored lower than the Befree on stability (7.0 vs 7.4) and overall (76 vs 80), was the slowest of the three to set up (14.5 s vs 12.0 s), and appeared 0.24 lb heavier in TechGearLab's table than its spec. Its case rests on packed shape, not measured stability. The Ulanzi Zero Y has no named measurement, so it can't be ranked on this angle.

findings.note: Stability is weighted 25% of the overall score. The test applied a few pounds of sideways pressure from every direction, took 1-second exposures in wind at three heights and ~20-second night exposures, and judged sharpness pass/fail. Listed con: 'So-so stability'. A tester said the centre column 'has a bit more flex than I'd like for long exposure photography.'
